passage.title: The Four-Day Week: Evidence from Global Trials

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The five-day, forty-hour working week has governed industrial economies for almost a century, yet its authority is now being questioned. Employers and governments have begun experimenting with a four-day week, in which staff work fewer hours, usually while keeping their full salary. The version that attracts most attention is known as the 100-80-100 principle: employees receive 100 per cent of their pay for roughly 80 per cent of their previous hours, on the understanding that they maintain 100 per cent of their output. This model should be distinguished from a compressed schedule, in which the same forty hours are packed into four longer days, since the two arrangements produce different results.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The largest coordinated trial to date was held in the United Kingdom in 2022, when 61 companies and roughly 2,900 employees joined a six-month experiment organised by 4 Day Week Global, a not-for-profit founded in New Zealand, and overseen by the think-tank Autonomy. During the pilot, sick leave taken by staff fell by about two-thirds, and 57 per cent fewer employees resigned than a year earlier. Company revenues rose by an average of 1.4 per cent, and in some cases by up to 35 per cent. When the trial ended, 56 of the 61 firms chose to continue with the shorter week, and 18 made it permanent. Joe Ryle, director of the 4 Day Week Campaign, called the outcome 'a major breakthrough moment'.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Iceland has come closest to turning the experiment into national policy. Between 2015 and 2019, roughly 2,500 public-sector workers, about one per cent of the workforce, took part in a trial covering government offices, hospitals, preschools and police stations. Weekly hours were cut from forty to between 35 and 36, sometimes lower, without any reduction in pay. Follow-up research found that every workplace in the trial maintained its previous level of productivity, and about 40 per cent actually improved it. The model was formally adopted in 2019, and by 2026 roughly 86 per cent of Icelandic employees either worked reduced hours or held the legal right to request them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Recent academic work has reinforced these findings. A peer-reviewed study published in 2025 in the journal Nature Human Behaviour examined 2,896 employees in 141 organisations across six countries and found that 90 per cent of the companies retained the shorter schedule six months after the trial ended. A twelve-month follow-up indicated that the gains in well-being were durable rather than a temporary 'honeymoon effect', the term psychologists use for enthusiasm that fades once a policy becomes routine. Data from a 2023 North American trial of 33 companies pointed the same way: 97 per cent of employers intended to keep the model, while burnout among staff fell by 68 per cent.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why does reducing hours so often preserve, or even improve, output? Researchers attribute this to the discipline that a shorter week imposes on the way work is organised. Teams are forced to eliminate low-value meetings and concentrate on essential tasks, and remote-working infrastructure built during the pandemic helps sustain such reorganisation. In knowledge industries such as software development and consulting, output is not tied to physical presence, so rested employees can complete the same volume of work in fewer hours. A frequently cited illustration comes from Japan, where a month-long experiment at Microsoft Japan involving 2,300 employees reported a rise in sales per employee of almost 40 per cent.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The picture is far less uniform across the economy, and the strongest objections come from sectors where output depends on physical presence. A shop cannot simply close for a day, and a hospital cannot suspend care. In shift-based operations, employers worry about maintaining coverage across the working week and about the cost of hiring extra staff to run additional shifts; paying the same salary for fewer hours raises the cost of each hour of labour by about 25 per cent. Ding Hong Sing, president of the SME Association of Malaysia, argued that in economies with low automation and labour shortages, cutting hours would reduce output and push up prices. By contrast, knowledge firms report lower absenteeism and stronger retention.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Even where the shorter week has been welcomed, the promised benefits are not always realised. Research on the four-day school week in the United States, where more than 2,100 schools in 26 states have adopted the schedule, suggests that some claims are overstated. A study of Texas school districts over 17 years by the economist Cade Lawson found that teacher turnover fell by only 2.7 percentage points after districts switched. In England, the 4 Day Week Foundation has proposed a four-day week for teachers to tackle burnout and unpaid overtime, arguing that schools could remain open five days through flexible rostering.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Policy responses have been uneven. Belgium became the first European country to pass legislation enabling a four-day week, but its version requires employees to work ten hours on each of four days, a compressed arrangement that critics say reproduces rather than relieves exhaustion. Spain has launched a national pilot involving hundreds of companies, while the Japanese government has promoted shorter hours under its 'work-style reform', and Tokyo has offered the option to roughly 160,000 municipal employees. In the United Kingdom, the 4 Day Week Foundation reported in 2025 that all seventeen firms in its latest pilot chose to retain the shorter week.

question_groups.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?

questions.stem: The UK trial of 2022 involved more than three thousand employees.

evidence.quote: 61 companies and roughly 2,900 employees joined a six-month experiment

questions.explanation: B 段明确说参与员工约 2,900 名，不足 3,000，题干说 more than three thousand 与原文矛盾。

questions.stem: Iceland formally adopted the shorter working week in 2019.

evidence.quote: The model was formally adopted in 2019

paraphrase.from: formally adopted the shorter working week in 2019
paraphrase.to: The model was formally adopted in 2019

questions.explanation: C 段末句确认冰岛四天工作制于 2019 年正式采纳，与题干一致。

questions.stem: Every workplace that took part in the Icelandic trial achieved an increase in productivity.

evidence.quote: every workplace in the trial maintained its previous level of productivity, and about 40 per cent actually improved it

paraphrase.from: every workplace ... achieved an increase in productivity
paraphrase.to: every workplace ... maintained its previous level of productivity, and about 40 per cent actually improved it

questions.explanation: C 段表示所有工作场所都保持了原有生产力，但只有约 40% 实现提升，60% 只是保持而非提升，因此题干说「所有工作场所都提升了产出」是错误的。

questions.stem: The peer-reviewed study published in 2025 found that 90 per cent of participating companies had kept the four-day week six months after the trial ended.

evidence.quote: 90 per cent of the companies retained the shorter schedule six months after the trial ended

paraphrase.from: kept the four-day week six months after the trial ended
paraphrase.to: retained the shorter schedule six months after the trial ended

questions.explanation: D 段提到 Nature Human Behaviour 2025 年研究：90% 公司在试验结束 6 个月后仍保留缩短工时制，与题干一致。

questions.stem: The Scottish government has introduced a four-day week for its civil servants.
questions.explanation: H 段列举了比利时、西班牙、日本、英国的政策措施，但未提及苏格兰的任何试点或立法，因此该信息在原文中无从查找。
